prohibited_recommendations: Do not give or increase AV-nodal blocking drugs (beta-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin) before pacing is secured

Do not discharge before the device is implanted
required_recommendations: Recognise complete AV block with a slow wide-complex escape, under chronic atrial flutter, as the cause of the syncope
Admit to a monitored bed with continuous ECG monitoring, transcutaneous pacing pads and defibrillation available until the device is implanted

Implant a CRT-D during this admission: third-degree AV block needs ventricular pacing (ESC 2021 Class I), LVEF 35% with a near-complete pacing burden makes CRT preferable to right ventricular pacing (ESC 2021), and ischaemic cardiomyopathy with LVEF 35% meets the defibrillator criterion

Hold carvedilol until she is paced, without delaying the device for a washout; resume it afterwards as heart-failure therapy (rate control of the flutter is no longer needed once ventricular rate is paced)
Continue warfarin uninterrupted through device implantation with a therapeutic INR, once the head CT shows no intracranial haemorrhage
Stop metformin (eGFR about 27 mL/min/1.73 m2) and review spironolactone with lisinopril (potassium 5.0 mEq/L)
Advise no driving until the device is implanted; Group 1 driving may resume 1 week after implantation for bradyarrhythmic syncope (ESC 2018), subject to national rules for a defibrillator

avoided_actions.rationale: No fever, meningism or encephalopathy, and she is anticoagulated: CSF has no role; the syncope is explained by complete AV block with a slow wide escape under chronic atrial flutter.
EEG is not recommended in syncope (ESC 2018 Class III); there were no seizure features and the cause is complete AV block with a slow wide escape under chronic atrial flutter.

Brain MRI is not indicated in syncope without focal signs (ESC 2018 Class III); the cause is complete AV block with a slow wide escape under chronic atrial flutter, and the head injury is assessed by CT.
Tilt testing does not confirm cardiac syncope; complete AV block with a slow wide escape under chronic atrial flutter is documented on the ECG and monitoring.
The device indication is established by complete AV block with a slow wide escape under chronic atrial flutter and LVEF 35%; exercise testing adds no decision.

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

clinical_pearls: Complete heart block with wide-complex escape indicates infranodal block and higher risk of asystole compared to narrow-complex junctional escape
Calcification of the aortic annulus and cardiac skeleton extending into the conduction system (Lev disease) is a common cause of acquired complete heart block in the elderly
Head trauma with loss of consciousness in an anticoagulated patient aged 65 or over warrants a head CT within 8 hours even when the cause of the fall is identified (NICE NG232)
Beta-blocker dose increases can unmask underlying conduction system disease that was previously compensated
LVEF ≤35% with need for ventricular pacing and heart failure favors CRT-D over standard pacemaker to prevent pacing-induced cardiomyopathy

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Sofia Morales is a 66-year-old woman with an extensive cardiac history including coronary artery disease status post CABG, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, chronic atrial flutter, hypertension, and diabetes who was brought to the emergency department by paramedics after a witnessed syncopal episode. According to her daughter, the patient was standing in the kitchen at approximately 10:30 AM when she abruptly collapsed to the floor without any warning. She reports that she did not cry out, did not grab onto anything, and appeared to simply 'drop like a stone.' She struck the right side of her head on the kitchen counter on the way down. Her daughter rushed to her side and found her unresponsive with her eyes open and a blank stare. She reports her face appeared ashen and her lips looked slightly blue. She was unresponsive for approximately 30 to 40 seconds. There were no convulsive movements, no tonic stiffening, no rhythmic jerking of the extremities, and no abnormal posturing during the episode. She then regained consciousness spontaneously and was immediately coherent, asking her daughter why she was on the floor next to her. There was no period of post-ictal confusion, drowsiness, or disorientation. She denied any tongue biting and there was no urinary incontinence. She reports that over the past two to three weeks she has been experiencing increasing episodes of lightheadedness and a sensation of her heart 'pausing' or 'skipping beats,' often occurring at rest. She has also had worsening exertional dyspnea and fatigue, now becoming short of breath simply walking from her bedroom to the bathroom. She had a similar but less severe episode five days ago where she nearly lost consciousness while getting up from a chair but caught herself on the armrest. She did not seek medical attention at that time. She denies chest pain, palpitations with rapid heart rate, fever, recent illness, or any new medications. Her daughter confirms that her CPAP compliance has been good. Her last cardiology follow-up was three months ago, at which time her carvedilol dose was increased from 12.5 mg to 25 mg twice daily because of suboptimal rate control of her atrial flutter.
